entities.summary:
Radegund was a Thuringian princess and Frankish queen who founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers in 570 AD, establishing a major center of Christianity in Gaul. This foundational act had significant consequences for the development of Christianity in Western Europe, as it brought together the Thuringian and Frankish Christian traditions under a single institutional framework. The Abbey of the Holy Cross played a crucial role in the early Middle Ages, serving as a center of learning, art, and spirituality that influenced the development of Western Christianity.

Radegund's significance extends beyond the Abbey of the Holy Cross, as she was a key figure in the transformation of the Frankish kingdom into a powerful Christian state. Her marriage to King Chlothar I and her influence on his policies marked a turning point in the history of the Franks, as they became a major force in Western Europe.

Radegund's legacy can be seen in the many churches and monasteries that she founded or influenced, including the Abbey of Saint-Denis and the Church of Saint-Radegund in Poitiers. Her life and legacy continue to inspire scholars and historians, offering a fascinating glimpse into the complex and often fraught history of early medieval Christianity.

The date of Radegund's death is not certain, but it is believed to have occurred in 587 AD, marking the end of an era that had a profound impact on the course of Western history.
